entities.name: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
observations: Irregular narrow-complex tachycardia with varying P-wave morphologies and variable PR intervals; commonly associated with COPD and hypoxemia.
Initial management focuses on correcting the underlying pulmonary trigger rather than synchronized cardioversion or amiodarone.

entities.name: COPD exacerbation
observations: Severe hypoxemic presentation with oxygen saturation 86% requires immediate controlled supplemental oxygen, titrated approximately to 88–92%.
NIPPV should be added promptly if hypoxemia, hypercapnic respiratory acidosis, increased work of breathing, or impending respiratory failure persists.

entities.name: Controlled supplemental oxygen
observations: Immediate priority in severe COPD exacerbation with SpO2 86%; titrate to approximately 88–92% while reassessing respiratory status.

entities.name: Non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation
observations: Escalation for persistent hypoxemia, hypercapnic respiratory acidosis, marked work of breathing, or impending respiratory failure after initial oxygenation.

entities.name: PMID:25447607
observations: Lambertz et al. studied fascial closure after open abdomen in a single-center retrospective cohort published in International Journal of Surgery in 2015. DOI: 10.1016/j.ijsu.2014.11.025.

entities.name: Open abdomen closure cohort
observations: Among 355 adults treated from 2003–2013, definitive fascial closure occurred in 137 (39%) and did not occur in 218 (61%).
An initially performed open abdomen was more common in the closure group: 97/137 (71%) versus 118/218 (54%), p=0.002.
Earlier second-look operations were associated with closure: 2.7±2.5 versus 4.2±6.6 days, p=0.021.
Earlier third-look operations were associated with closure: 5.6±3.7 versus 8.5±8.6 days, p=0.006.

The authors concluded that initial open-abdomen strategy and early second- and third-look revisions increase the probability of fascial closure; pancreatitis was the only reported negative prognostic marker. The retrospective design supports association, not definitive causation.
